meta.author: Shashi Kumar
meta.summary: Cross-interview review while redesigning search and the property page. Gaps: almost nothing on how students filter, sort, use the map or shortlist; nobody has watched a student use the property page; findings skew to agents and Amber+; sample is mostly India-to-UK bookers recruited via agents, with nobody from Pakistan or Nigeria. What held up: videos and viewings matter but are hard to find (Videos chip 0.41% usage); parents often decide and students screenshot rather than share (share button 0.24%); nobody uses the chatbot (9/9 interviews, 1-2% on site); people compare on distance, privacy and cost over WhatsApp, and on-site comparers enquire 5-8x more. Suggestions: recruit from site behaviour (comparers, lost leads, parents, Nigeria, Pakistan, US), run screen-share sessions with real tasks, default to video calls with past-tense open questions, and update the themes doc after every call. Harshal replied suggesting Shashi run a few interviews himself (1793703682.968319).

interviews.summary: Jaipur student going to Leeds for an international business master's, persuaded to study in the UK by a childhood friend. The CRM referrer was wrong: his friend Lakshya, an Amber agent, handled the whole booking, so it was not a self-serve conversion. The March-May gap was spent waiting on a bank loan, and he never looked at competitors.
context: Booked Burley Road, Leeds Bronze Ensuite, 51 weeks at £118/week; deposit paid via Revolut after one failed attempt.
CRM shows referral from Atin Jangid, zero agent calls, and booking within 48 hours of lead creation.
First WhatsApp activity was on 12 Mar, seven weeks before the lead was created.

points.text: A childhood friend who graduated from Bristol and works at Amazon convinced him; employment outcomes were the main pull.
He applied late for Bristol and settled on Leeds, with other offers in hand.
He was waiting for an education loan from Union Bank of India, whose assessment year closed on 31 March.
Lakshya, an Amber agent and his personal friend, referred him and handled form filling and payment.
He did not explore competitors because Lakshya works at Amber.
He did not know the CRM referrer, Atin Jangid.
The agent promised cashback, so the new lead was created with an earlier lead's referral details; referrer, referee and agent all get rewarded.
He is waiting for loan disbursement before applying for his visa and is using IDP for admission fees and visa formalities.

insights.text: His long gap was waiting on a bank loan, not indecision.
The CRM referrer was wrong; the real referrer was an Amber agent who is his friend.
Agents can create leads with another lead's referral details so cashback gets paid.
A friend's job outcome after a UK degree drove his decision to study abroad.
An insider agent did the whole booking, so 'zero calls' in the CRM did not mean self-serve.
He relies on IDP for admission fees and visa formalities.

actionables.text: Audit referral attribution where agents create leads using another lead's referral details.
actionables.rationale: The CRM named a referrer the student had never heard of.

actionables.text: Document the rules for agent referrals and incentives.
actionables.rationale: Shreyas could not find how agent referrals and bonuses work.

actionables.text: Time nurture messages around loan sanction for loan-dependent students.
actionables.rationale: His booking moved as soon as the loan was sanctioned.

actionables.text: Find the root cause of his failed first payment.
actionables.rationale: Deepesh asked for it as a follow-up.

actionables.text: Write a 'High-Intent Referral User' persona note comparing this journey with the average funnel.

gaps.text: CRM referral attribution can be wrong when agents reuse referral details.
Agent-handled bookings look self-serve in the CRM.

interviews.summary: Kenyan nursing student already living in Birmingham who came to Amber through friends to secure next year's room early and avoid price rises. She wanted a viewing that the property never confirmed over two months and then booked privately. She has little free time, low tolerance for multi-step tools, and valued her university portal showing roommates before move-in.
context: Lost in March with reason 'booked private accommodation'.
Wanted an ensuite at £140-150/week and asked to view before booking; the agent spent two months trying to arrange it.
Created about 8 duplicate leads across properties on one night.
Interview pushed from 8 to 9 Apr.

points.text: Kenyan nursing student at Birmingham, in the UK since Sep 2025, with hospital shifts, classes and church on Sundays.
She uses WhatsApp, phone alarms and smartwatch reminders, and avoids apps like Google Calendar.
points.quote: too many steps involved.

points.text: Friends told her about Amber; she has used the website but never the chatbot.
She booked her first year through the university portal, which showed potential roommates before move-in.
Safety and certainty, not price, drove that choice.
She came in February to book next year's room early to beat price inflation and save money.

insights.text: An unmet viewing request over two months pushed her to a private rental.
She has very little tolerance for multi-step tools.
She heard about Amber from friends.
Seeing roommates before move-in on the university portal set her benchmark.
Safety and certainty drove her first booking.
She came early to lock in next year's price.
She has never used the chatbot.

actionables.text: Offer video or virtual viewings when a property cannot confirm an in-person viewing.
actionables.rationale: Two months without a viewing lost her to a private rental.

actionables.text: Show potential flatmates before move-in where providers allow it.
actionables.rationale: Her university portal did this and it set her expectations.

actionables.text: Promote early booking for next year with price protection to students already in the UK.
actionables.rationale: She came to beat price inflation.

actionables.text: Keep booking steps short and send reminders over WhatsApp.
actionables.rationale: She drops tools that take too many steps and lives on WhatsApp.

gaps.text: Amber could not deliver a viewing the student asked for.
Students can't see future flatmates before booking.

interviews.summary: Investment banker heading to Warwick for a master's, who booked Millennium View at £99/week as part of a group of three. Discovery was peer-led (seniors, Unibuddy), the group compared 3-4 properties by sharing links on WhatsApp, and reviews didn't help because almost all were similarly positive. His post-booking stress is administrative (visa, loan, exams) because he applied without a consultant.
context: Booked Millennium View, Coventry Silver Ensuite, 51 weeks at £99/week; stated budget £205/week.
Came in through a referral chain; two of his referrals also booked; booked the same evening he first contacted Amber.
His only lead-form question was how many people share the kitchen.
Call pushed from 16:00 and ran 17:00-17:40.

points.text: Investment banker doing a master's for better pay, who also wants to unwind, enjoy and learn about other cultures.
Seniors and other communities helped him decide on- vs off-campus.
He found batchmates through Unibuddy, which his university told him about.
A group of 3 decided over WhatsApp: seniors had stayed at Millennium, transport and groceries/pharmacy were sorted, and it was 50% under budget.
They shortlisted and compared properties on WhatsApp by sharing links.
About 98% of properties had similarly high ratings, so reviews didn't differentiate; he cross-checked on Google.
points.quote: ~98% of properties had similarly high and positive ratings

points.text: He wanted to meet people from different cultures and backgrounds, not people from his own city.
He never used the chatbot and only looked at 3-4 properties.
Visa, loan and exams are stressful without a consultant.
He wants customizable student kits and discovered kits on Instagram.

insights.text: Discovery was peer-led through seniors and Unibuddy, not platform-led.
The group decided over WhatsApp using seniors' experience, transport, groceries and price.
Uniformly high ratings made reviews useless for deciding, so he checked Google.
He wanted a culturally diverse place to build his network.
He never used the chatbot.
Applying without a consultant left him stressed about visa, loan and exams.
He wants customizable student kits and found out about kits on Instagram.

actionables.text: Offer visa and loan guidance for students applying without a consultant.
actionables.rationale: Admin tasks are his main stress.

actionables.text: Show resident mix or community information on the property page.

interviews.summary: PhD student in food science going to Leeds, who found Amber via Google and was already in the UK staying in an Airbnb. A guarantor requirement was a major blocker despite a fellowship, and the booking fell through when the property manager hadn't received Amber's referral on move-in day and he couldn't reach Amber outside working hours. He found the chatbot too rule-based and preferred human agents.

points.text: PhD student (Food Science and Nutrition) going to Leeds; visa done; found Amber organically on Google.
He relied heavily on Google ratings to compare and was influenced by agent Sugandh and friends.
Proximity to university, amenities such as a gym, accurate listing photos and budget.

He strongly preferred human help for high-value decisions and rated the agent highly.
